Dear Pinecrest Insights Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the Data Analyst (New Grad, 2027) role. I'm a senior at Brookfield University studying Computer Science with a minor in Data Science, and I graduate in May 2027. I've spent the last year working with data in two settings. As an intern I built dashboards, and as a research assistant I worked with interview data from teens. Pinecrest's work with education, healthcare, and nonprofit clients would let me keep doing both.

Last summer I was a Data Analyst Intern at Brightpath Learning, an ed-tech company. I built a Tableau dashboard that tracked weekly active students, lessons completed, and learning streaks for the product team. I also wrote the SQL for the tables behind it. The hardest part was the data itself. When the app went to the background, it split one session into several, so sessions were being double-counted. I redefined a session as activity with gaps of less than 30 minutes, using window functions over the event timestamps. After that fix, the numbers matched how students actually used the app. My manager found the breakdown of streaks by grade level especially useful.

Since October 2025, I've been an undergraduate research assistant in Brookfield's Social Computing Lab. I work on a PhD-student-led interview study about how teens aged 15–17 use online communities for mental-health support. I sent recruitment messages and ran the eligibility screener. I transcribed and de-identified 14 interviews, and I coded 6 transcripts with the team's codebook. In our inter-rater reliability check we reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.71 after one round of reconciliation. This work taught me to handle sensitive youth data carefully, and it gave me hands-on practice with the qualitative coding your survey work involves.

In a team machine learning project, we fine-tuned a transformer to classify sentiment in Reddit support posts. It reached a macro-F1 of 0.81, compared with 0.72 for a TF-IDF baseline. I led the error analysis. I found that the model often labeled sarcastic or dark-humor posts as negative. That was a good reminder that the numbers only mean something once you understand the people behind them.

I'd be glad to bring SQL, Python, Tableau, and qualitative research skills to a Pinecrest client team, and to learn from your mentorship program. Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
Avery Santos

I've written this as a draft for you to react to, not a final version. A statement of interest has to name a research direction and the faculty you want to work with, and I can't settle either of those for you. In October you told me you didn't have a clear research question yet, and that you weren't sure whether you like the lab's topic or mostly like working with J. Kim. So I built the direction from the two moments in our past chats where you sounded most engaged: the sarcasm errors you found in the ML error analysis, and the coding disagreements you wanted to write memos about. If that direction isn't true to you, it'll show in interviews, and we should change it.

---

**Statement of Interest — PhD in Human-Computer Interaction, Khoury College of Computer Sciences**

In my machine learning course, my team fine-tuned a transformer to classify sentiment in Reddit mental-health support posts. On paper it worked: macro-F1 of 0.81, compared with 0.72 for a TF-IDF baseline. But when I did the error analysis, I found a pattern the score hid. The model kept labeling sarcastic and dark-humor posts as negative. People in support communities often use humor to talk about hard things, and some of those posts were the writer coping, connecting with others, or making light of something painful. The model read those posts as distress. I want to study that gap between how people actually talk about their struggles online and how computational systems interpret what they say.

**Research experience**

Since October 2025, I've been an undergraduate research assistant in the Social Computing Lab at Brookfield University with Prof. A. Moreno. I work on an interview study led by PhD student J. Kim about how teens aged 15–17 use online communities for mental-health support. My role was supporting, not leading, and it gave me close contact with the data at every stage. I sent recruitment messages to community moderators and ran the eligibility screener. I transcribed and de-identified 14 of the 16 interviews, which meant replacing names, schools, and server names with placeholders while keeping the meaning of what participants said. I then coded 6 transcripts with the team's codebook. In our inter-rater reliability check with J. Kim, we reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.71 after one round of reconciliation. The paper is now under review, and I'm listed in the acknowledgments.

The coding taught me the most. Our disagreements were rarely careless mistakes. They usually came from passages where a teen's tone was ambiguous: a joke that might have been a disclosure, or a complaint about a community that was also a sign of belonging to it. Resolving those passages took discussion and context that a single label couldn't capture. It was the same problem I had seen in the classifier, this time from the human side.

**Technical and applied background**

I'm finishing a B.S. in Computer Science with a minor in Data Science, and I've taken Intro to HCI and a seminar in Social Computing. Last summer I was a Data Analyst Intern at Brightpath Learning, an ed-tech company. I built a Tableau dashboard of student engagement and wrote the SQL behind it. That included fixing double-counted sessions by defining a session from the gaps between events. The internship showed me how much a single measurement decision can change what an organization believes about its users. It's a smaller version of the question I want to study.

**Research interests**

During a PhD, I want to combine qualitative and computational methods to understand how young people express distress, humor, and support in online communities, and how automated systems such as moderation tools, content classifiers, and recommendation systems read and respond to that expression. Questions I'm curious about include:

- When do automated systems misread coping or community humor as risk, and what happens to teens and moderators when they do?
- How can qualitative insights, like the ambiguities we argued over while coding, shape how these systems are designed and evaluated?
- How do we study this kind of data responsibly, given that it comes from minors and is sensitive by nature?

I don't have a fixed project yet, and I expect these questions to change through coursework and work with an advisor. I'm drawn to them because they draw on both kinds of work I've done so far: carefully reading what people say, and building systems that try to do the same thing at scale.

**Why Khoury**

[FACULTY FIT — 1 paragraph. Name 1–2 Khoury HCI faculty, cite a specific paper or project of theirs, and say how it connects to the questions above. Placeholder: see note below.]

Khoury's HCI program would let me build on my training in computer science while getting deeper training in qualitative and human-centered methods. Being in Boston would also give me access to the wider research community working on youth, technology, and wellbeing.

**Goals**

After the PhD, I hope to do research in academia or in an industry research group, working on how online platforms can better support the people who turn to them in difficult moments.

---

**What you'd need to fill in or check:**

1. **Is the research direction yours?** I made it up from your ML error analysis and the coding disagreements. If something else actually excites you, tell me and I'll rewrite the opening and the research interests section.
2. **Faculty fit is blank on purpose.** My search only reliably turned up Tianshi Li, whose PEACH Lab works on HCI, AI, and privacy. That could connect to the responsible-data question, but it's a loose fit. Please browse the Khoury HCI faculty pages and tell me who you'd actually want to work with, or ask J. Kim, who will probably know who's a good fit.
3. **Prompt and length.** I couldn't load Khoury's application page. Check the official prompt and word limit. This draft is about 800 words.
4. **Your role.** I described your RA work as supporting and gave specific details, so it holds up even though you didn't lead anything. Prof. Moreno's letter should back that up, so it's worth sending them this draft.
5. **Something I left out.** You once said one of the interviews "stuck with" you. A personal moment like that can make a statement much stronger, but whether to share it is up to you, so I didn't use it.

---

**Statement of Interest — PhD in Human-Computer Interaction, Khoury College of Computer Sciences**

One of the teens in an interview study I worked on told us about an online server that was the only place she felt she could admit she was having a bad day. Then the moderators added a bot that automatically deleted posts containing certain words, and some of her posts disappeared. [*If approved: She described it as "being shushed by a robot."*] I understand why the moderators did it. They were volunteers trying to keep a vulnerable community safe, and automated filters are one of the few tools that scale. But her account has stayed with me, and so has a question it raised: when moderation tools are built to manage risk, who are they actually serving, and what do they teach young people about what is okay to say when they need help?

I want to pursue a PhD in HCI to study how automated moderation shapes the way teens seek support online. I'm especially interested in whether these tools change what teens feel able to disclose, and how they might be designed with the people asking for help in mind.

**Research experience**

Since October 2025, I've been an undergraduate research assistant in the Social Computing Lab at Brookfield University, working with Prof. A. Moreno on an interview study led by PhD student J. Kim. The study looks at how teens aged 15–17 use online communities for mental-health support. My role was supporting, not leading, and it kept me close to the data at every stage. I sent recruitment messages to community moderators and ran the eligibility screener. I transcribed and de-identified 14 of the 16 interviews, replacing names, schools, and server names with placeholders while keeping the meaning of what participants said. I then coded 6 transcripts with the team's codebook. In our inter-rater reliability check with J. Kim, we reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.71 after one round of reconciliation. The paper is under review, and I'm listed in the acknowledgments.

Transcribing taught me to listen closely to how teens talk about hard things. Coding showed me how often that talk is ambiguous. Most of our disagreements were about tone: whether a joke was also a disclosure, or whether a complaint about a community was also a sign of belonging to it. We could only resolve those passages through discussion and context.

**Computational background**

I saw the same ambiguity from the other side in my machine learning course. My team fine-tuned a transformer to classify sentiment in Reddit mental-health support posts and reached a macro-F1 of 0.81, compared with 0.72 for a TF-IDF baseline. I led the error analysis and found that the model consistently labeled sarcastic and dark-humor posts as negative. Those are the posts where people are often coping, and where coders like me had to slow down and think. A word filter is much simpler than that model, but it faces the same problem: it reacts to the words people use, not to what they mean or need.

I'm finishing a B.S. in Computer Science with a minor in Data Science, with coursework in HCI and social computing. Last summer, as a Data Analyst Intern at Brightpath Learning, I built a Tableau dashboard of student engagement and the SQL behind it. Part of that work was fixing double-counted sessions by redefining what counts as a session. It taught me how much a single definition built into a system shapes what an organization believes about the people using it.

**Research interests**

I'm still forming my question, and I expect it to change with coursework and an advisor. These are the directions I'm drawn to now:

- How do teens experience automated moderation in support communities? Do filters change what they disclose, how they phrase it, or whether they post at all?
- How do volunteer moderators weigh safety, liability, and the needs of members who are asking for help, and where do automated tools fit into those decisions?
- What would moderation tools look like if they were designed with the people seeking support, not only for the people managing risk?

I'd like to approach these questions with qualitative methods, such as interviews with teens and moderators, alongside computational analysis of how moderation systems behave.

**Why Khoury and Prof. Li**

I'm particularly interested in working with Prof. Tianshi Li. The PEACH Lab argues that AI systems need human-centered approaches that empower the people affected by them, not only better models, and that is how I think about automated moderation. A filter's accuracy matters, but so does whether the teen whose post disappears understands what happened and has any say in it. [*Add one sentence naming a specific PEACH Lab paper or project you've read and how it connects.*] I would bring experience with sensitive qualitative data from young people, and I'd hope to learn from the lab's rigor in studying how people experience AI systems. More broadly, Khoury's HCI program would let me build on my computer science training while getting deeper grounding in human-centered research methods.

**Goals**

After the PhD, I hope to do research in academia or in an industry research group, helping online platforms support the people who turn to them in difficult moments instead of silencing them.

---

**Before submitting:**

Last winter I transcribed interviews with teens about how they use online communities when they're struggling. Then the moderators added a bot that automatically deleted posts with certain words, and some of hers just disappeared. [*If J. Kim approves: She called it "being shushed by a robot."*]

I get why the mods did it. They're volunteers trying to keep people safe, and a word filter is one of the few tools they have. But I keep wondering who those tools are really for. Are they protecting the teens who are posting, or mainly the people responsible for the space? And if your posts keep disappearing, what does that teach you about what you're allowed to say when you need help? That question is the main reason I'm applying.

I had run into the same thing in a machine learning class project, where my team built a classifier for Reddit support posts. My favorite part was the error analysis, because the model kept marking sarcastic or dark-humor posts as negative. Those are often the posts where someone is coping. A word filter is far simpler than that model, but I think it has the same problem: it reacts to the words people use, not to what they mean.

I don't have a research question yet so much as things I keep wondering about. How do teens notice and react when their posts are filtered? Do they rephrase, go quiet, or leave? How do moderators decide where to draw the line? And could these tools be built with the people asking for help in mind, not just the people managing risk? I'd want to start by talking to teens and moderators, but I know I have a lot to learn about how to study this well, especially with young people.

Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment

Zhiping Zhang, Franklin Mingzhe Li, Raio Zihao Huang, Tianshi Li

Preprint

When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. Each task is specified by an authorization contract that separates the principal's instruction, completion criteria, and out-of-authorization actions. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged (19.3% at low effort versus 19.1% at high effort), with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p = 0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment, motivating it as a distinct target for agent evaluation and development. AgentDoxx: Agentic Re-identification of Anonymized Text with Web Search

Jianing Wen, Tianshi Li

Preprint

As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain tool use capabilities such as web search, they can retrieve and cross-reference public information, creating privacy risks beyond memorization. One manifestation is re-identification: linking an anonymized interview transcript to a named individual. Yet without ground-truth identities, the coverage of such attacks and the protection offered by a defense cannot be reliably measured. We introduce AgentDoxx, an evaluation suite of 822 synthetic interview transcripts grounded in public information about real individuals with known identities. We evaluate fifteen configurations of open-weight and proprietary models, isolating the effect of web search, and analyze their search trajectories to distinguish retrieval-driven from parametric identifications. Ground-truth identities reveal that re-identification risk is distributed across an agent's execution: retrieval and parametric recall both contribute, with open-weight models identifying 15-28% of transcripts without search; identification succeeds in over 88% of cases once the target appears in a retrieved result; entity masking leaves at least one attacker successful on 85.3% of a stratified sample; and privacy instructions suppress naming but not retrieval, with configurations scoring 0% accuracy yet retrieving the subject in up to 62% of transcripts. We further show that observed attack trajectories can provide supervision for localizing identifying spans, offering a path toward attack-informed anonymization.

LLM agents require personal information for personalization in order to effectively act on users' behalf, but this raises privacy concerns that can discourage data sharing, limiting both the autonomy levels at which agents can operate and the effectiveness of personalization. We conducted a 3×3 between-subjects experiment (N=450) to study how agent autonomy level influences personalization's effects on users' privacy concerns, trust, and willingness to use, as well as the underlying psychological processes. We find that risk-contingent autonomy, where the agent delegates control back to users upon detecting potential privacy leakage, improves users' perceived control. This in turn attenuates personalization's adverse effects: privacy concerns rise less and trust declines less. Our results suggest that designing agent's autonomy that supports human autonomy (both perceived control and oversight effectiveness) helps users benefit from personalization without being deterred by growing privacy concerns. This positions aligning decision authority between users and agents (autonomy alignment) as an important opportunity and challenge for trustworthy human-agent interaction.

Bingcan Guo, Eryue Xu, Jijie Zhou, Zhiping Zhang, and  Tianshi Li

In COLM 2026 Oct 2026

Abs arXiv Dataset Code

Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human privacy preferences requires capturing individuals’ disclosure boundaries beyond general privacy norms. However, current models lack methods for eliciting such nuanced preferences and ground truth data to evaluate alignment in realistic settings. We introduce CIDER, a dataset of 14,850 human annotations from 169 users, forming 1,650 contextual disclosure boundary sets across 60 interpersonal communication scenarios where information sharing violates privacy norms. Each boundary represents a real user’s disclosure decisions over 9 sharing variants, given a communication role and AI-mediated condition. We formulate a prediction task in which models predict a user’s disclosure decision from historical boundaries, with varying levels of contextual information. Across eight open and proprietary models, personalization improves performance, with accuracy gains of up to 11.41% using six in-context examples. However, these gains arise from different mechanisms. Larger models such as GPT-5.4 (with medium reasoning effort) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 leverage semantic context to infer user-specific, context-dependent disclosure preferences for more accurate predictions, while smaller models tend to rely on structured heuristics based on disclosure granularity and identifiability and present trade-offs between false positives and false negatives. Our findings highlight the potential and limitations of current LLMs’ privacy modeling capability and position CIDER as a resource for advancing personalized privacy preference alignment.

We present a framework to formally define and operationalize data minimization: for a given user prompt and response model, quantifying the least privacy-revealing disclosure that maintains utility, and propose a priority-queue tree search to locate this optimal point within a privacy-ordered transformation space. We evaluated the framework on four datasets spanning open-ended conversations (ShareGPT, WildChat) and knowledge-intensive tasks with single-ground-truth answers (CaseHOLD, MedQA), quantifying achievable data minimization with nine LLMs as the response model. Our results demonstrate that larger frontier LLMs can tolerate stronger data minimization while maintaining task quality than smaller open-source models (85.7% redaction for GPT-5 vs. 19.3% for Qwen2.5-0.5B). By comparing with our search-derived benchmarks, we find that LLMs struggle to predict optimal data minimization directly, showing a bias toward abstraction that leads to oversharing. This suggests not just a privacy gap, but a capability gap: models may lack awareness of what information they actually need to solve a task.

Results reveal that people rely on ad hoc manual strategies while lacking comprehensive privacy controls, highlighting nine privacy-management challenges across applications, temporal contexts, and relationships. To explore solutions, we generated nine AI agent concepts and evaluated them via a speed-dating survey with 116 US participants. The three highest-ranked concepts were all post-sharing management tools with half or full agent autonomy, with users expressing greater trust in AI accuracy than in their own efforts. Building ethical LLM-based CAs that respect user privacy requires an in-depth understanding of the privacy risks that concern users the most. However, existing research, primarily model-centered, does not provide insight into users’ perspectives. To bridge this gap, we analyzed sensitive disclosures in real-world ChatGPT conversations and conducted semi-structured interviews with 19 LLM-based CA users. We found that users are constantly faced with trade-offs between privacy, utility, and convenience when using LLM-based CAs. However, users’ erroneous mental models and the dark patterns in system design limited their awareness and comprehension of the privacy risks. Additionally, the human-like interactions encouraged more sensitive disclosures, which complicated users’ ability to navigate the trade-offs. We discuss practical design guidelines and the needs for paradigmatic shifts to protect the privacy of LLM-based CA users.

IMWUT

Matcha: An IDE Plugin for Creating Accurate Privacy Nutrition Labels

Tianshi Li , Lorrie Faith Cranor, Yuvraj Agarwal, and Jason I Hong

Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol. Apr 2024

Abs arXiv HTML Website

Apple and Google introduced their versions of privacy nutrition labels to the mobile app stores to better inform users of the apps’ data practices. However, these labels are self-reported by developers and have been found to contain many inaccuracies due to misunderstandings of the label taxonomy. In this work, we present Matcha, an IDE plugin that uses automated code analysis to help developers create accurate Google Play data safety labels. Developers can benefit from Matcha’s ability to detect user data accesses and transmissions while staying in control of the generated label by adding custom Java annotations and modifying an auto-generated XML specification. Our evaluation with 12 developers showed that Matcha helped our participants improved the accuracy of a label they created with Google’s official tool for a real-world app they developed. We found that participants preferred Matcha for its accuracy benefits. Drawing on Matcha, we discuss general design recommendations for developer tools used to create accurate standardized privacy notices.

CHI

Understanding Challenges for Developers to Create Accurate Privacy Nutrition Labels

Tianshi Li , Kayla Reiman, Yuvraj Agarwal, Lorrie Faith Cranor, and Jason I Hong

In CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems Apr 2022

Best Paper Honorable Mention Award 🏅

📰 Media coverage: The Washington Post , Consumer Reports

Abs HTML PDF

Apple announced the introduction of app privacy details to their App Store in December 2020, marking the first ever real-world, large-scale deployment of the privacy nutrition label concept, which had been introduced by researchers over a decade earlier. The Apple labels are created by app developers, who self-report their app’s data practices. In this paper, we present the first study examining the usability and understandability of Apple’s privacy nutrition label creation process from the developer’s perspective. By observing and interviewing 12 iOS app developers about how they created the privacy label for a real-world app that they developed, we identified common challenges for correctly and efficiently creating privacy labels. We discuss design implications both for improving Apple’s privacy label design and for future deployment of other standardized privacy notices.

IMWUT

Honeysuckle: Annotation-Guided Code Generation of In-App Privacy Notices

Tianshi Li , Elijah B Neundorfer, Yuvraj Agarwal, and Jason I Hong

Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol. Sep 2021

Abs HTML PDF Talk Demo

In-app privacy notices can help smartphone users make informed privacy decisions. However, they are rarely used in real-world apps, since developers often lack the knowledge, time, and resources to design and implement them well. We present Honeysuckle, a programming tool that helps Android developers build in-app privacy notices using an annotation-based code generation approach facilitated by an IDE plugin, a build system plugin, and a library. We conducted a within-subjects study with 12 Android developers to evaluate Honeysuckle. Each participant was asked to implement privacy notices for two popular open-source apps using the Honeysuckle library as a baseline as well as the annotation-based approach. Our results show that the annotation-based approach helps developers accomplish the task faster with significantly lower cognitive load. Developers preferred the annotation-based approach over the library approach because it was much easier to learn and use and allowed developers to achieve various types of privacy notices using a unified code format, which can enhance code readability and benefit team collaboration.

PMC

What makes people install a COVID-19 contact-tracing app? Understanding the influence of app design and individual difference on contact-tracing app adoption intention

Tianshi Li , Camille Cobb, Jackie (junrui) Yang, Sagar Baviskar, Yuvraj Agarwal, Beibei Li, Lujo Bauer, and Jason I Hong

Pervasive Mob. Comput. Aug 2021

Best Research Paper 2019-2021 Award 🏆

Abs HTML PDF

Smartphone-based contact-tracing apps are a promising solution to help scale up the conventional contact-tracing process. However, low adoption rates have become a major issue that prevents these apps from achieving their full potential. In this paper, we present a national-scale survey experiment (N=1963) in the U.S. to investigate the effects of app design choices and individual differences on COVID-19 contact-tracing app adoption intentions. We found that individual differences such as prosocialness, COVID-19 risk perceptions, general privacy concerns, technology readiness, and demographic factors played a more important role than app design choices such as decentralized design vs. centralized design, location use, app providers, and the presentation of security risks. Certain app designs could exacerbate the different preferences in different sub-populations which may lead to an inequality of acceptance to certain app design choices (e.g., developed by state health authorities vs. a large tech company) among different groups of people (e.g., people living in rural areas vs. people living in urban areas). Our mediation analysis showed that one’s perception of the public health benefits offered by the app and the adoption willingness of other people had a larger effect in explaining the observed effects of app design choices and individual differences than one’s perception of the app’s security and privacy risks. With these findings, we discuss practical implications on the design, marketing, and deployment of COVID-19 contact-tracing apps in the U.S.

CSCW

How Developers Talk About Personal Data and What It Means for User Privacy: A Case Study of a Developer Forum on Reddit

Tianshi Li , Elizabeth Louie, Laura Dabbish, and Jason I Hong

Proc. ACM Hum. Comput. Interact. Jan 2021

Abs HTML PDF Talk

While online developer forums are major resources of knowledge for application developers, their roles in promoting better privacy practices remain underexplored. In this paper, we conducted a qualitative analysis of a sample of 207 threads (4772 unique posts) mentioning different forms of personal data from the /r/androiddev forum on Reddit. We started with bottom-up open coding on the sampled posts to develop a typology of discussions about personal data use and conducted follow-up analyses to understand what types of posts elicited in-depth discussions on privacy issues or mentioned risky data practices. Our results show that Android developers rarely discussed privacy concerns when talking about a specific app design or implementation problem, but often had active discussions around privacy when stimulated by certain external events representing new privacy-enhancing restrictions from the Android operating system, app store policies, or privacy laws. Developers often felt these restrictions could cause considerable cost yet fail to generate any compelling benefit for themselves. Given these results, we present a set of suggestions for Android OS and the app store to design more effective methods to enhance privacy, and for developer forums(e.g., /r/androiddev) to encourage more in-depth privacy discussions and nudge developers to think more about privacy.

IMWUT

Coconut: An IDE Plugin for Developing Privacy-Friendly Apps

Tianshi Li , Yuvraj Agarwal, and Jason I Hong

Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol. Dec 2018

Abs HTML PDF Demo Website

Although app developers are responsible for protecting users’ privacy, this task can be very challenging. In this paper, we present Coconut, an Android Studio plugin that helps developers handle privacy requirements by engaging developers to think about privacy during the development process and providing real-time feedback on potential privacy issues. We start by presenting new findings based on a series of semi-structured interviews with Android developers, probing into the difficulties with privacy that developers face when building apps. Based on these findings, we implemented a proof-of-concept prototype of Coconut and evaluated it in a controlled lab study with 18 Android developers (including eight professional developers). Our study results suggest that apps developed with Coconut handled privacy concerns better, and the developers that used Coconut had a better understanding of their code’s behavior and wrote a better privacy policy for their app. We also found that requiring developers to do a small amount of annotating work regarding their apps’ personal data practices during the development process may result in a significant improvement in app privacy.

Its main topics are data minimization, AI agents acting without permission, and re-identification. Content moderation doesn't appear anywhere, so the email shouldn't pretend the fit is closer than it is.

- **De-identification.** AgentDoxx and the related re-identification papers show that simply masking names in interview transcripts often isn't enough to stop AI tools from identifying people. That's exactly the de-identification you did by hand.
